stops.name: Leon, the surname and the gap behind it
stops.date_confidence: traditional; c.1240 is an estimate with no document behind it, and the day and month are placeholders. Bar-Asher and Brown (2025) prefer 'Moses de Leon of Guadalajara', holding that only the family, not necessarily the man, is documented as coming from Leon. Both positions are stated; neither is chosen here.
stops.campa: A boy is born somewhere in the Kingdom of Castile and will carry the name of this city for the rest of his life and for seven centuries after it. That is close to the whole of what the record holds. The year is an estimate. Nobody wrote down the birthplace, and the mother and the first teachers are gone past recovery. His father survives only as a patronymic fastened to a son: Moshe ben Shem Tov de Leon. The newest scholarship would rather call him Moses de Leon of Guadalajara and let the surname stand for the family alone.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'
Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (Oxford University Press, 2025)
Jewish Encyclopedia, on the patronymic ben Shem Tov
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of medieval Leon, beside the cathedral

stops.name: Guadalajara, the Guide copied for him
stops.date_confidence: attested by manuscript colophon; the year is firm, the day and month are placeholders, and the city is inferred from Guadalajara being the best-attested centre of his activity rather than named in the colophon itself. The manuscript was not located and no shelfmark was found for this file.
stops.campa: A scribe finishes a copy of Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed and records that it was made for Moses de Leon. It is the earliest thing anyone can prove he owned, the first hard date in his life, and a floor under everything before it. What it shows is a young man buying philosophy: God argued rather than seen, Aristotle carried north through Cordoba and Fustat. Maimonides has been sixty years dead and never travelled to Castile in his life. The book comes anyway. The colophon gives the year, 1264. It does not give a month, and it does not name the town it was written in.
sources: Manuscript colophon evidence cited in Scholem and in Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025)
Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'
suggested_refs: maimonides.journey.json, for the Fustat years in which the Guide was written
The thirteenth-century Castilian circulation of the Guide of the Perplexed in Hebrew translation

stops.name: Guadalajara, Gikatilla and the two Kabbalahs
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The relationship with Gikatilla is traced by Bar-Asher and Brown (2025) through parallel passages, not by any document placing the two men together. Gikatilla was born at Medinaceli, worked chiefly at Segovia, and died at Peniafiel; no source has him living at Guadalajara. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He comes into the orbit of Joseph Gikatilla, who works out of Segovia and who has studied under Abraham Abulafia. They begin by disagreeing. Gikatilla builds from the letters of the alphabet, their permutations and their numbers; Moses builds from the sefirot, the ten graded powers through which the hidden God is said to act on the world. No document puts the two men in one room. What can be traced is the writing: across the 1280s the positions bend toward each other until each man's books carry the other's marks.
sources: Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025)
Wikipedia, 'Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla'
suggested_refs: Joseph Gikatilla, Ginnat Egoz and Sha'are Orah
Abraham Abulafia's combinatorial letter-permutation technique, taught to Gikatilla c.1272-74

stops.name: Guadalajara, what Girona and Burgos send him
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dated only to order the segment. He is not recorded travelling to Girona, Burgos, or Toledo, and no stop is staged at any of them; the debts are traced by parallel passages in his own books, which is how most medieval influence is traced at all.
stops.campa: Into his synthesis run currents he did not begin. From Girona comes the theosophical Kabbalah of Ezra and Azriel, where the sefirot are the inner life of God rather than tools God reaches for; from Burgos, the harder Castilian speculation of Moses of Burgos on the powers of the left side. Todros Abulafia is at Toledo. What arrives is not the men but their sentences, copied out and carried by whoever was going that way. He is not on record travelling to Girona, to Burgos, or to Toledo, and the debts are read off his own pages.
sources: Scholem-school genealogies of Gerona Kabbalah
Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025)
suggested_refs: Ezra and Azriel of Girona, the theosophical circle of the early thirteenth century
Moses of Burgos on the emanations of the left

stops.name: Guadalajara, the Nameless Composition
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The work is unsigned; its attribution to him is Bar-Asher and Brown's (2025). The research pool tied it to the court of Sancho IV; the Oxford abstract for Light is Sown places it instead in 'Alfonsine Castile's cultural context', and 1284 falls exactly on the reign boundary and cannot arbitrate. Sancho IV is dropped. No source names Moses de Leon as holding any office at any court.
stops.campa: An unsigned Hebrew work goes into circulation, reconstructed seven centuries later as an early book of his own. Penitence runs through it: the mechanics of turning back, what a soul does when it returns. It is written inside the weather of Alfonsine Castile, where a king has spent thirty years having Arabic and Hebrew learning put into the vernacular and where a Jewish scholar with a patron writes for readers who are not all Jews. He does not put his name on it. The attribution is Bar-Asher and Brown's, made in 2025 out of style and doctrine.
sources: Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025), on the Nameless Composition
Oxford University Press abstract, DOI 10.1093/oso/9780197744819.001.0001
suggested_refs: The translation workshops of Alfonso X at Toledo and Seville
The penitential thread running from the Nameless Composition into Mishkan ha-Edut

stops.name: Toledo, the patron in the house of Abulafia
stops.date_confidence: the patronage is attested; his physical presence at Toledo is not. No record places Moses de Leon in the city, and this stop marks where the patron and the dedications are, not a documented residence. The date orders the segment. Coordinate corrected to the Sinagoga del Transito per OpenStreetMap.
stops.campa: Joseph ben Todros ha-Levi Abulafia keeps him. Patronage in thirteenth-century Castile means a household that pays for parchment and a copyist and expects books addressed to it, and this household is a kabbalistic one in its own right, kin to Todros Abulafia. Nothing in the record puts Moses himself in the city. What can be shown to have gone the hundred kilometres southwest from Guadalajara is the work: finished quires, tied, carried down the Toledo road by whoever was going.
sources: Standard biographical summaries of Moses de Leon (Scholem; Bar-Asher and Brown)

segments.name: The Book in Another Man's Voice

stops.name: Guadalajara, the Aramaic begins to move
stops.date_confidence: inferred. Not one sheet of the Zoharic material carries a date, a colophon, or a signature; the 1280s placement rests on when it is first reported circulating and on its relation to the dated Hebrew treatises. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Sheets begin moving through Castile written in an Aramaic nobody has spoken for a thousand years, presenting themselves as the work of Shimon bar Yochai, the second-century sage of the Galilee, set down in a cave with his son beside him. The grammar goes wrong in places no native would err. Arabic and Castilian sentence shapes show through the weave. Moses de Leon never claims to have written a word of it. He says there is an old manuscript, and that it is at his house.
stops.quote: some said Shimon ben Yochai had never written this book, but that Moses had written these wonderous words and falsely ascribed them to Shimon ben Yochai and his son Elazar in order to sell them for huge sums of money
stops.quote_source: One of the reports Isaac of Acre says he heard circulating, as excerpted in Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
sources: Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941), on the Aramaic grammar and the Arabic and Spanish sentence patterns
Isaac of Acre, as excerpted in Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89

stops.name: Guadalajara, the Galilee he has never seen
stops.date_confidence: inferred, dated only to order the segment. The unfamiliarity with the Land of Israel's real geography is one of the standing arguments against the corpus being ancient; it is an argument about the text, not a dated event in his life.
stops.campa: The book walks Shimon bar Yochai and his companions along roads between Galilean towns, arguing Torah under trees, stopping at wells, and it gets the country wrong. The distances do not work. The landscape is assembled out of the Talmud rather than out of a horizon anyone has stood in front of. He is writing a land he will never see, from a town in Castile, in the language of a Babylonia he will never see either. Whether that is ignorance or a decision about how a holy country ought to look on the page, the text does not say.
sources: Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)
Wikipedia, 'Zohar', on the geographical unfamiliarity argument
suggested_refs: Eitan Fishbane, The Art of Mystical Narrative: A Poetics of the Zohar (Oxford, 2018)
rabbi_shimon_bar_yochai_rashbi.journey.json, for the Galilean geography the Zohar reconstructs from memory of a text

stops.name: Guadalajara, shem ha-kotev
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. This is an emic explanation reported to Isaac of Acre by informants after the death, recorded as a period belief about him and not as evidence of any technique. Placed here to sit beside the output it was invented to explain; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Informants will later tell Isaac of Acre that the output is not natural. They say Moses composes by shem ha-kotev, the Name of the Writer, a power that lays words down faster than a hand can invent them. It is the explanation people reach for when one man in a provincial town produces, inside a single decade, a shelf of signed Hebrew treatises and a vast Aramaic literature in a dead sage's voice. It reaches Isaac second-hand and after the funeral, and it records what people believed about him rather than anything he said about himself.
sources: Traditions transmitted within the Isaac of Acre material, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857)
Standard Zohar-authorship scholarship summaries
suggested_refs: The shem ha-kotev tradition as discussed in Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)

stops.name: Guadalajara, quires that do not yet make a book
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, following Daniel Abrams, 'The Invention of the Zohar as a Book' (Kabbalah 19, 2009). The date is an ordering device; the claim is about the form of the corpus, not about a dated event.
stops.campa: What leaves his hands is not a book. It is units: homilies on the Torah portions, the Idrot, the Sifra di-Tseni'uta, the Midrash ha-Ne'lam, more than twenty distinguishable groupings that travel as separate quires and get copied in whatever order a buyer's scribe happens to work in. A Zohar with a spine and a fixed table of contents is an achievement of sixteenth-century printers. Daniel Abrams made that argument in 2009 out of the manuscripts, which do not agree with one another about what the book contains.
sources: Daniel Abrams, 'The Invention of the Zohar as a Book', Kabbalah 19 (2009)
Ronit Meroz, stratigraphic manuscript studies
suggested_refs: The Pritzker Edition (Stanford University Press, 2004-2017), built from manuscripts rather than the printed vulgate
Yehuda Liebes, 'How the Zohar Was Written', in Studies in the Zohar (SUNY, 1993)

stops.name: Guadalajara, Shoshan Edut
stops.date_confidence: attested by colophon; the year is firm, the day and month are placeholders.
stops.campa: This one he signs. Shoshan Edut, the Lily of Testimony, in Hebrew, under his own name, dated. It opens a run of treatises that will come out of this house at roughly one a year for seven years. The signed Hebrew and the unsigned Aramaic are being written in the same room in the same years, on the same doctrines, in two voices: a Castilian rabbi explaining the sefirot to his contemporaries, and a Galilean sage overheard eleven centuries too late. The colophon gives 1286, without a day or a month.
sources: Dated colophon of Shoshan Edut
Inventory of Moses de Leon's signed Hebrew corpus in Wolfson and in Bar-Asher and Brown (2025)
suggested_refs: The signed Hebrew corpus as the control text for every argument about Zoharic authorship

stops.name: Guadalajara, Sefer ha-Rimmon
stops.date_confidence: attested by colophon; the year is firm, the day and month are placeholders.
stops.campa: The Book of the Pomegranate: a long treatise on the reasons for the commandments, worked out through the sefirot and through a sexual symbolism in which the male and female sides of the godhead reach for each other, so that a commandment performed below repairs the union above. The same theme is being worked in the Aramaic in the same years, each body of writing taking up what the other has just found. Elliot Wolfson establishes the Hebrew text in 1988 and sets it beside the Zoharic passages line for line.
sources: Elliot Wolfson, critical edition of Sefer ha-Rimmon (1988)
Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025), on gender symbolism
suggested_refs: Elliot Wolfson's critical edition of Sefer ha-Rimmon (1988), the text against which Zoharic parallels are read

stops.name: Guadalajara, Or Zaru'a
stops.date_confidence: attested by colophon evidence, conventionally dated 1288-1289; the day and month are placeholders.
stops.campa: Or Zaru'a, Light is Sown, follows the Rimmon inside a year or two. The title comes out of a psalm: light is sown for the righteous. Seven centuries later Bar-Asher and Brown will take the same phrase for the title of the book that reconstructs his mind out of these treatises. He is turning out a signed Hebrew treatise about once a year while telling people that his own part in the Aramaic is to hold an old manuscript somebody else wrote. The colophon evidence gives 1288 or 1289 and nothing sharper.
sources: Dated colophon evidence for Or Zaru'a, discussed in Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025)
suggested_refs: Psalm 97:11, the source of the title and of Bar-Asher and Brown's own

stops.name: Guadalajara, Ha-Nefesh ha-Hakhamah, for a pupil named Jacob
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the colophon, which names the pupil Jacob; the year 1290 is the conventional dating and the day and month are placeholders. Nothing further about Jacob is recorded anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: The colophon names the person it is for: Jacob, his student. It is one of the very few places in the whole record where his audience is a human being with a name rather than a reconstruction from the argument. The book treats the soul, its parts, and what becomes of it once the body is finished, with the punishments and the returns set out at length. The same ground is worked in the Aramaic and put into Shimon bar Yochai's mouth. Nothing else about Jacob is recorded anywhere.
sources: Colophon of Ha-Nefesh ha-Hakhamah, naming the pupil Jacob
Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025)
suggested_refs: The Zoharic homilies on the soul's parts, developed on the same ground in the same years

stops.name: Guadalajara, Shekel ha-Kodesh
stops.date_confidence: attested by colophon; the year is firm, the day and month are placeholders.
stops.campa: The Shekel of the Sanctuary, on the sefirot and on the weighing of things against a fixed standard. It closes the tightly dated sequence. After this year the colophons thin out and the itinerary opens instead: Valladolid, then Avila, then the road between them ridden more than once. He is around fifty-two, if the traditional birth year holds, and he will not stay anywhere long again. Six signed treatises have come out of this house in seven years, each dated, each under his own name, and there will be one more.
sources: Dated colophon of Shekel ha-Kodesh
Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'

stops.name: Guadalajara, Mishkan ha-Edut and a contested year
stops.date_confidence: contested and left open. The research pool's chronology gives 1290; its own geography lens hedges to 'early 1290s'; the conventional dating is 1293, used here as an ordering date. No source consulted supports 1290. Bar-Asher's 2013 critical edition is cited as the pool gives it but could not be confirmed in Crossref or Open Library.
stops.campa: The Tabernacle of the Testimony, on the soul and on repentance, carrying forward the penitential thread that first showed in the unsigned early work. Between this book and the unsigned early one, penitence becomes a visible through-line in his own thought, one of the threads later used to argue that a single mind is developing across the writing rather than copying an older book. Bar-Asher's critical edition gives the text. The year is not agreed: some inventories say 1290, the conventional dating says 1293, and nothing consulted here decides between them.
sources: Bar-Asher, critical edition of Mishkan ha-Edut (2013), cited but unconfirmed in Crossref and Open Library
Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025), on penitential practice

stops.name: Guadalajara, Maskiyyot Kesef and the books that are gone
stops.date_confidence: attested as written after 1293; 1294 is an ordering date, not a dated colophon. The list of lost titles is unresolved: the bibliographies disagree with each other and one of them assigns him a book that belongs to Isaac ibn Sahula.
stops.campa: Maskiyyot Kesef, Settings of Silver, written some time after 1293, is among the last securely his. Other titles survive only as names inside other men's lists: Sefer ha-Pardes for certain, and then, depending which bibliography is trusted, Tappuhei Zahav, Sha'arei Tzedek, a commentary on the Song of Songs, a polemic against the Karaites. Not one of those books survives to be checked against the lists that name it. One list hands him Mashal ha-Kadmoni, which was written by Isaac ibn Sahula.
sources: Standard inventory of Moses de Leon's signed Hebrew works
he.wikipedia, 'Moshe de Leon', for the competing list of lost titles
Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941)

stops.name: Valladolid, the travel picks up
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1290s and 1300s in general; the specific year is an ordering device. No source records his reason for the shift, and none is inferred here.
stops.campa: Around 1291 or 1292 the travel picks up, and through the decade that follows he is repeatedly in Valladolid, the busiest court city in Castile. No source says why. Age, money, patrons who have to be visited, the ordinary itinerancy of a scholar who lives by teaching and copying: all of these have been proposed and not one of them is his own recorded reason. By the time he stops moving he has spent some thirty years between this city and Guadalajara.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'
Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown (2025), on the late itinerary
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Valladolid in the reign of Fernando IV

stops.name: Talavera, the test of Joseph ha-Levi
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the story is undated and reaches us only inside the Isaac of Acre material via Zacuto. The date orders the segment. The tradition that carries the test also carries the counter-reading, and this file does not choose between them.
stops.campa: Joseph ha-Levi of Talavera will tell Isaac of Acre that he tested him here. He asked Moses to reproduce from memory a passage his own copy was missing, then set the replacement against the original and found them the same, word for word. He took that for proof of the ancient book. The tradition that preserves the story preserves the objection alongside it, unresolved: a man who wrote the passage himself would need no memory at all, only his own master copy, kept at home.
sources: Tradition transmitted within the Isaac of Acre material, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
suggested_refs: The competing testimonies Isaac of Acre gathered after 1305, none of which he adjudicated in the surviving excerpt

stops.name: Avila, inside the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested that Avila is his home in the final years; the year of the move is not recorded and 1300 is an ordering date.
stops.campa: He moves inside the great granite ring of towers and settles for what is left. Avila is a walled town of perhaps ten thousand, its Jewish quarter pressed against the southern wall, and it holds the one thing the coming argument will turn on: his house, and whatever is or is not kept in it. From here forward, every question anyone asks about the Zohar has a street address to be asked at. He is past sixty, if the traditional year holds, and the dated colophons have stopped coming.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'
Isaac of Acre, as excerpted in Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
suggested_refs: The medieval walls of Avila and the juderia beneath them

segments.name: Isaac of Acre Comes to Check

stops.name: Valladolid, the man who came to check
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1305; the day and month are placeholders. Isaac's account survives only as an excerpt inside Abraham Zacuto's much later Sefer Yuhasin, printed 1566, censored out of the 1580 edition, and absent for roughly three centuries until Filipowski restored it in 1857.
stops.campa: Isaac ben Samuel of Acre reaches Castile. He was in Acre in 1291 when the Mamluk army took the town, was arrested and thrown in prison with the other Jews, escaped the massacre, and came west fourteen years afterward. He has read the sheets going around under Shimon bar Yochai's name and he wants to know where they came from. He finds Moses de Leon at Valladolid and asks him to his face. Neither man leaves a document behind. What survives is Isaac's own account, excerpted centuries later inside somebody else's chronicle.
stops.quote: And I went to Spain, to the capital city of Valladolid, and presented myself to Moses
stops.quote_source: Isaac of Acre, as excerpted in Abraham Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
sources: Isaac of Acre, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
Wikipedia, 'Isaac ben Samuel of Acre', on the 1291 fall of Acre and the 1305 journey to Spain
suggested_refs: The printing history of Sefer Yuhasin: Constantinople 1566, censored 1580, restored by Filipowski 1857

stops.name: Valladolid, the oath
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1305 within the same excerpt; the month is an ordering device and no source dates the exchange more closely than the year.
stops.campa: He swears it. The ancient book exists. It was written by Shimon bar Yochai's own hand. It is at his house in Avila and Isaac may come and see it. This is the strongest form the claim ever takes: sworn, to a man who has crossed the Mediterranean to test it, with a date set for the proof and a road agreed on. What is sworn to is not a doctrine but an object: parchment, in a room, in a walled town two days' ride south of here. Isaac hears the whole of it and stays where he is. Moses de Leon sets out for home.
stops.quote: Because I had seen that these words were wonderous, that they ran from a well high above which is beyond those uninitiated into the secrets of the divine, I chased after it
stops.quote_source: Isaac of Acre, on his own motive for pursuing the question, as excerpted in Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857)
sources: Isaac of Acre, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
suggested_refs: The road from Valladolid to Avila by way of Arevalo, some one hundred and forty kilometres

stops.name: Arevalo, the road not finished
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1305; the month is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected to 41.0632, -4.7199 per OpenStreetMap; the research pool carried two conflicting pins for the same town.
stops.campa: He falls ill on the way and dies at Arevalo, some fifty kilometres short of his own door at Avila and of the room the oath named, before any outside eye reaches the house. On the record that survives he never confesses to anything. To the last exchange anybody wrote down he maintains that the old manuscript is real and that he will produce it. What closes the question from his own side is not an admission but an illness on a road. No source names the illness, and none gives the day.
sources: Isaac of Acre, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'

stops.name: Avila, the widow and the daughter
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The report is undated and reaches Isaac through at least two intermediaries before Zacuto excerpts it centuries later; the month orders the segment. Neither the widow nor the daughter is named in any source consulted, though they are the only first-hand witnesses to what was in the house.
stops.campa: Isaac keeps asking after the death. Through an intermediary at Avila named David de Pancorbo, and through the wife of a certain Joseph of Avila, a report comes back out of the household: there was no ancient book. Moses wrote it out of his own head and put it in Shimon bar Yochai's mouth because his own name would not have sold it. At least three people stand between the widow and Isaac's page, and two and a half centuries between that page and any copy of it now readable. Neither the widow nor the daughter is named.
stops.quote: By the Lord, my husband never had such a book except in his mind, and everything he wrote came from his own intellect
stops.quote_source: The widow of Moses de Leon, reported through David de Pancorbo to Isaac of Acre, as excerpted in Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857)
sources: Isaac of Acre, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
Wikipedia, 'Isaac ben Samuel of Acre'
suggested_refs: The second reported line of the same confession: that for his own words they would not give a penny, but for the work of Shimon bar Yochai they will pay in blood

stops.name: Avila, Pancorbo's verdict
stops.date_confidence: attested as a first-person statement inside the Isaac of Acre excerpt, distinct from the widow's reported words; undated in the source, and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Pancorbo does not hedge. He tells Isaac flatly that no ancient manuscript ever reached this Moses's hands and that there is no Zohar except the one Moses wrote every word of. Isaac writes it down. Then Isaac goes on collecting, and the other testimonies do not agree with this one, and his own later book, Otzar HaHayim, states that the Zohar was written by Shimon bar Yochai after all. The surviving excerpt of the investigation breaks off before he says what he concluded.
stops.quote: Know in truth that it is clear to me beyond doubt that it never came to the hand of this Moses, and that there is no Zohar except that of which Moses himself wrote every word
stops.quote_source: David de Pancorbo to Isaac of Acre, as excerpted in Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857)
sources: Isaac of Acre, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
Isaac of Acre, Otzar HaHayim, per Wikipedia, 'Isaac ben Samuel of Acre'
suggested_refs: Otzar HaHayim, in which Isaac of Acre affirms the antiquity his own investigation had put in doubt

stops.name: Avila, the manuscript that came by wind
stops.date_confidence: legend, undated in the source; the month orders the segment. The stop sits at Avila because that is where the manuscript was said to be, and no stop is staged at Alicante, because nobody in the record travelled that route.
stops.campa: Another of the testimonies Isaac gathers runs the opposite way. The manuscript is genuine. It descended from Nahmanides, went from the Land of Israel into Catalonia and so into Castile. One version has it carried on the wind toward Aragon and the coast at Alicante, coming ashore there and finding its own way inland. The miraculous detail is the mark of the genre: this is a story about a relic rather than a chain of custody. How the book gets from that beach to a house at Avila, no teller explains, and Isaac writes the version down without pressing anyone on it.
sources: Isaac of Acre, via Zacuto, Sefer Yuhasin, ed. Filipowski (1857), pp. 88-89
suggested_refs: The Gerona Kabbalah of Nahmanides, to which the legend attaches the manuscript's descent

stops.name: Arevalo, no stone
stops.date_confidence: stated gap, not a dated event; the date is an ordering device. The absence of any burial record is confirmed across en., es., and de. wikipedia, and no primary burial document was located.
stops.campa: There is no grave. No headstone, no burial register, and no plot anyone can point at. The medieval Jewish cemetery of Arevalo did not come through 1492 intact, and where in it he was laid is written down nowhere. No source gives the day he was buried, or the rite, or who stood at the edge of it. Everything anyone knows of the man is in the writing, and the writing is the thing under dispute. Seven centuries on, Guadalajara will put up a bronze of him. Arevalo has nothing.
sources: Standard biographical consensus (Scholem; Bar-Asher and Brown, Light is Sown, 2025); no primary burial record located
Wikipedia, 'Moses de Leon'
suggested_refs: The 1492 expulsion and the loss of the Castilian Jewish cemeteries

stops.name: Guadalajara, what the printers made of the quires
stops.date_confidence: posthumous by two and a half centuries, and staged at his own pin because it concerns the object he made rather than the printers who made it into a book. The pool called Mantua the first edition; en.wikipedia gives Cremona 1558 in one volume beside Mantua 1558-1560 in three, it.wikipedia dates Cremona to 1560, and Tikkunei haZohar was printed at Mantua in 1557 before any of them. Zohar Hadash was printed first at Salonika, 5357, and only then at Krakow, 5363.
stops.campa: The quires come back together in Italy, and not as one book. Cremona prints a Zohar in a single volume; Mantua prints a different Zohar in three; Salonika gathers the material left outside both and calls it Zohar Hadash, and Krakow reprints that a few years later. The editions disagree with each other about what belongs inside. What he released in loose quires is being assembled by men who are strangers to him by two and a half centuries. Mantua's page numbers become the standard citation and are still it.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Zohar', printing history
it.wikipedia, 'Zohar', dating Cremona to 1560
Daniel Abrams, 'The Invention of the Zohar as a Book', Kabbalah 19 (2009)
suggested_refs: The Soncino Press English translation by Sperling, Simon, and Levertoff (London, 1931-1934)
The Pritzker Edition, twelve volumes, Daniel C. Matt with Nathan Wolski and Joel Hecker (Stanford University Press, 2004-2017)

stops.name: Guadalajara, another man's book under his name
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1605 printing; the reattribution is Scholem's judgement and is not universally followed, since later catalogues go on listing the book as his. Staged at his own pin because it concerns his name, not the press.
stops.campa: Sefer ha-Shem is printed in 1605 with his name on the title page. The man who spent his working life putting his own words into a dead sage's mouth acquires, three centuries after dying, a book he did not write. Gershom Scholem examines it and gives it to a different, later Moses, on the grounds he uses everywhere: language, doctrine, and the fit or misfit with the treatises that carry a signature. Not everyone follows him. Later catalogues go on listing the book as this Moses de Leon's.
sources: Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941), bibliographic notes on Sefer ha-Shem
suggested_refs: The 1605 printing of Sefer ha-Shem and its persistence in later catalogues of his works

stops.name: Guadalajara, the bronze on the avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested. It is a bust, not a statue, one of nine bronzes commissioned by the municipal government along the Avenida de Francisco Fernandez Iparraguirre. The plaque's claim that he was born at Guadalajara is a local assertion, not the scholarly position, and is flagged rather than cited as evidence.
stops.campa: The city sets nine bronze busts along the Avenida de Francisco Fernandez Iparraguirre and one of them is his. Luis Sanguino casts it in 2003, and it is the only monument to him anywhere. Scholarship does not say he was born here. It says this is where he worked, and where nearly everything datable in his life was written. The town has settled the question in its own favour, in bronze. The plaque reads: philosopher and rabbi, born in Guadalajara, author of the Book of Splendour, rule of the Kabbalah.
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Luis Sanguino', on the 2003 bronze bust and the nine-bust commission
suggested_refs: The nine bronze busts of the Avenida de Francisco Fernandez Iparraguirre, Guadalajara

stops.name: Guadalajara, four answers still standing
stops.date_confidence: posthumous scholarship, staged at his own pin. Every scholar named belongs in sources and suggested_refs rather than in a scene, and none of them is staged at their own city here. The four hypotheses are given as live because no source consulted closes between them.
stops.campa: The argument has run without a break since Leone Modena wrote against Kabbalah at Venice in 1639, through Luzzatto and Jellinek and Graetz, through Scholem's ruling in 1941 that Moses de Leon wrote the main body of it alone, through Liebes's circle of companions and Abrams's book that was never a book until printers made it one. Four answers are still standing: he wrote it, he compiled it, he transmitted something older, he worked inside a Castilian circle. Bar-Asher and Brown return it to him in 2025 without restoring sole authorship.
